items.title: Sailing along a constant compass bearing draws a spiral around the pole
items.claim: A 'rhumb line' (loxodrome) is a path that crosses every meridian at the same angle — what you sail if you hold a constant compass course. Except for due east/west (the equator) or due north/south, a rhumb line spirals around the pole, eventually reaching it after infinite winding.
items.prompt: Why doesn't a constant bearing give a great circle?

options.text: Great circles change bearing as you traverse them (except along the equator or meridians); to maintain a constant compass bearing, you must follow a different curve that spirals — the loxodrome
It only happens near the pole

items.reveal:
A loxodrome (rhumb line) is the curve that intersects all meridians at the same angle. On a sphere, this is an equiangular spiral.

For any constant bearing not aligned with the equator or a meridian, the path spirals around the pole. The length to reach the pole is finite (the spiral converges) but the number of windings is infinite.

On a Mercator projection, rhumb lines appear as straight lines — this is the property Mercator designed his projection for in 1569. Hold a ruler against a Mercator chart and you have a constant compass bearing course.

Great circles, by contrast, appear as curves on Mercator maps, generally bowed toward the nearer pole. Modern aviation uses great-circle routes; old-school open-ocean sailing used rhumb lines (easier to navigate without constant heading recalculation).

In practice: long-distance navigation often combines them — fly an approximate great circle, but compute waypoints at intervals (e.g., every 5 degrees of longitude) and sail rhumb lines between waypoints. This is 'composite sailing'.

The loxodrome was first studied by the Portuguese navigator Pedro Nunes (1537). It contributed to the systematic mathematisation of navigation in the Age of Discovery.
items.why: Compasses point to magnetic north. Holding a constant bearing draws a curve that no Euclidean intuition prepares you for — and the difference between loxodrome and great circle has shaped maps, navigation, and naval strategy for centuries.

items.title: Most people earn less than the average wage
items.claim: If you tell people the 'average wage' in their country, most of them are below it. This isn't a fluke — it's a feature of skewed distributions like income, where a few huge values pull the mean up but most observations sit lower.
items.prompt: What's the difference that matters here?

options.text: There is no difference — these terms are interchangeable
Mean (arithmetic average) is pulled by extreme values; median (50th percentile) splits the population in half; for income distributions, the mean is well above the median because of high earners

items.reveal:
Three common 'averages':
- Mean: sum of values divided by count. Sensitive to extreme values.
- Median: the middle value when sorted. Robust to extremes.
- Mode: the most common value. Useful for categorical data.

For a symmetric distribution (like adult height), mean ≈ median ≈ mode. The 'typical' person is well-described by any of them.

For skewed distributions:
- Right-skewed (income, wealth, city size): mean > median > mode. A few huge values pull the mean up.
- Left-skewed (test scores with a ceiling): mean < median.

US household income (2022): mean ~115,000 USD, median ~75,000. The 'average household' as measured by mean is income that 60% of households fall below.

Dangers of using mean carelessly: 'the average net worth in this room is 100 million USD' (because Elon Musk just walked in). For policy and individual planning, median is often more informative.

The terms have legal force: a statement that 'most people earn the average wage' is misleading for income, even if it would be roughly true for height.
items.why: 'Average' has many meanings, and in skewed distributions they diverge dramatically. Almost every report on income, wealth or wait times that uses the word 'average' should be parsed carefully.

items.title: Ice cream sales correlate with drownings — neither causes the other
items.claim: When ice cream sales rise, drowning deaths rise. Strong correlation. Both peak in summer. Neither causes the other — they share a common cause (hot weather drives both ice cream consumption and swimming).
items.prompt: What's wrong with inferring causation from correlation?

options.text: Correlation can arise from: X causes Y; Y causes X; both have a common cause (confounder); selection bias; chance. Without further evidence (experiment or careful causal modelling), we cannot distinguish which
Causation always implies correlation, so causation and correlation are the same

items.reveal_title: Hill criteria, confounders, and the structure of causal inference
items.reveal:
Correlation = statistical association. Causation = mechanistic dependence.

Reasons for correlation without direct causation:
- Common cause (confounder): heat causes both ice cream sales and drownings.
- Reverse causation: rooster crowing 'causes' the sun to rise? Actually opposite.
- Selection bias: hospitalised patients show that brain injury and dietary habits correlate, but only because they were both selected by the hospital criteria.
- Coincidence: with enough variables, spurious correlations are inevitable (https://tylervigen.com/spurious-correlations).

Establishing causation usually requires:
1. Randomised controlled experiment: randomly assign causes, observe effects. Eliminates confounders by design.
2. Natural experiments: variation in cause that's plausibly random (timing of policy changes, weather).
3. Bradford Hill criteria (1965): strength, consistency, specificity, temporality, biological gradient, plausibility, coherence, experiment, analogy. Used in epidemiology when RCTs aren't possible.
4. Causal inference frameworks (Pearl's directed acyclic graphs, potential outcomes).

Famous miscalls:
- Hormone replacement therapy and heart disease (observational said 'protective'; RCT said 'harmful').
- Vitamin E and cancer prevention (observational said 'protective'; RCT said 'no effect').
- Coffee and heart disease (many flip-flops).

The replication crisis in psychology and biomedicine partly reflects systematic overinterpretation of correlation as causation.

When RCTs aren't possible (ethics, scale), causal inference is harder but not impossible — but requires careful design and explicit assumption-naming.
items.why: 'Correlation implies causation' is a famous fallacy — but the converse fallacy ('all correlations are meaningless') is also wrong. Understanding the structure of causal evidence is key to scientific literacy.
